hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? have you ever felt you’d gone too far down the wrong road to turn back?
options: then this story is for you. listen.
then listen for them. this one is hopeful.
good. listen anyway. you’ll meet someone who did.

steps.line: The Talmud tells of Rabbi Yochanan, a great scholar, famous for his beauty. One day he was bathing in the Jordan River.
A bandit named Reish Lakish saw him and, in one great leap, jumped into the river after him.

steps.q: A powerful bandit lands in the river beside the rabbi. What does Rabbi Yochanan say?
steps.why: He saw strength, not just a bandit. And he told him where it could go.

steps.line: Rabbi Yochanan looked at him and said, “Your strength should be for Torah.” Reish Lakish shot back, “Your beauty should be for women!”

steps.q: The bandit teases the rabbi about his looks. How does the rabbi win him over?
o: Promises him a seat in the study hall
Offers his even more beautiful sister
Offers to pay off his debts
steps.why: His sister, “more beautiful than I am.” The Talmud tells it with a grin: the rabbi answers the bandit in the bandit’s own terms.

steps.line: “If you turn around,” said the rabbi, “I’ll give you my sister in marriage, and she is more beautiful than I am.” Reish Lakish agreed.
He tried to go back for his things, and couldn’t. Rabbi Yochanan taught him, and he became one of the great sages of his time.

steps.q: Reish Lakish tried to leap back across for his clothes, and couldn’t. How do the commentators explain it?
o: The river had risen in the night
Taking on Torah had sapped his old strength
Rabbi Yochanan held on to him
steps.why: The Talmud says only that he couldn’t. Rashi explains: once he took on Torah, the old bandit’s strength was already draining. The old life had closed behind him.

steps.line: Later, Reish Lakish himself taught: when a person turns back out of love, even their worst wrongs become merits.

steps.q: Years later, Rabbi Yochanan got a new study partner who agreed with everything he said. How did he feel?
steps.why: “Reish Lakish would raise twenty-four objections,” he said, “and from the answers the law grew clear” (Bava Metzia 84a). The bandit’s strength became the sharpest mind in the room.

steps.line: Today, the month before the Jewish new year, and the ten days up to Yom Kippur, are set aside for teshuvah. But the door stays open any day.
steps.label: today

say: here’s what i love. teshuvah comes from shuv, to turn. it doesn’t say you’re broken. it says you’re facing the wrong way, and you can turn around.

maimonides laid out how: stop, regret it honestly, say it out loud, and decide not to do it again. and the rabbis said that where someone who has returned stands, even the completely righteous can’t stand.

steps.q: The rabbis taught that teshuvah was created before the world itself. What might that mean?
o: God expected people never to stray
The way back came before the first wrong
Only the first humans could return
steps.why: Pesachim 54a lists seven things made before the world, teshuvah among them, with the Torah and the Garden of Eden. The road home was built before the first wrong turn.

today.say: pick one small habit you’d like to turn from. today, try maimonides’ first steps: stop once, and say out loud, to yourself or someone you trust, what you’re turning from. that’s teshuvah, out of your head and into words.
options: say it out loud. that’s the turn beginning.
good. naming it is where the turn starts.
